pragmatism: Pragmatism is a philosophical tradition, largely American in origin, that judges the meaning and worth of ideas by their practical consequences rather than by their correspondence to a fixed reality. Emerging in the late nineteenth century through the work of Charles Sanders Peirce, William James, and John Dewey, it holds that beliefs are tools for coping with experience and that a theory's value lies in how well it guides action and inquiry. Against the search for absolute, timeless truths, pragmatists treat knowledge as provisional, revisable, and continuous with everyday problem-solving.
pragmatic-method: The pragmatic method, first sketched by Charles Sanders Peirce, is a rule for clarifying the meaning of a concept by tracing the practical effects we would expect if it were true. To grasp what an idea signifies, one asks what observable differences it would make in experience and conduct; if two rival notions imply no such difference, they mean the same thing. Peirce intended this as a discipline for settling otherwise interminable metaphysical disputes by tying meaning to conceivable consequences.
will-to-believe: The will to believe is William James's argument that in certain cases we are entitled to adopt a belief on faith, before the evidence is conclusive, when the choice is genuine, momentous, and cannot be settled by intellect alone. James responded to the demand that we withhold assent until proof arrives, contending that some truths—especially moral and religious ones—only become available to those willing to commit in advance. Refusing to decide, he noted, is itself a choice with consequences, so passionate belief can be legitimate rather than a lapse in reason.
stream-of-consciousness: Stream of consciousness is William James's term for the continuous, flowing character of mental life, in which thoughts and sensations run together rather than arriving as discrete, separable units. In his Principles of Psychology he argued that experience is felt as an unbroken current, always personal, always changing, and never the same twice, so the mind cannot be analyzed into a mosaic of fixed atoms. The idea reshaped psychology and later gave its name to a literary technique for rendering the movement of inner experience.
pragmatic-truth: Truth as what works is the pragmatist account, developed especially by William James, that a belief is true insofar as it proves useful in guiding us successfully through experience. Rather than defining truth solely as a static match between statement and fact, James held that ideas become true through a process of verification—they "work" by leading to reliable expectations and satisfactory dealings with the world. Critics charged that this confuses truth with mere expediency, and James spent much effort insisting that genuine working must answer to reality, not personal convenience.
dewey-democracy: Democracy as a way of life is John Dewey's conviction that democracy is not merely a form of government but a mode of shared, cooperative living rooted in communication, inquiry, and mutual respect. For Dewey, self-rule means people continually participating in the associations that shape them—workplaces, schools, communities—and reconstructing those institutions through intelligent, experimental problem-solving. On this view voting and elections are only the outer machinery; the deeper substance is a culture in which individuals grow by contributing to and learning from a common life.
dewey-experience: Experience and education names John Dewey's philosophy of learning, which holds that genuine education grows out of and reorganizes lived experience rather than transmitting inert facts. Reacting against both rote traditional schooling and unstructured permissiveness, Dewey argued that educative experiences must be continuous, connecting to what came before and opening onto further growth, and interactive, engaging the learner with a real environment. Teaching, in this scheme, is the thoughtful arranging of conditions so that students inquire, test ideas, and develop the habits of intelligent reflection.
emerson-self-reliance: Self-reliance is the ideal Ralph Waldo Emerson championed in his 1841 essay of that name: the summons to trust one's own intuition and conscience rather than conform to society's expectations, traditions, or the opinions of others. Emerson urged that each person carries an original relation to truth and that imitation is a kind of suicide of the soul, so integrity means acting from inner conviction even at the cost of appearing inconsistent. The doctrine celebrates individual nonconformity as the wellspring of genuine thought and moral courage.
transcendentalism: Transcendentalism was a nineteenth-century American intellectual and literary movement, centered in New England, that emphasized the primacy of intuition, the divinity of nature, and the inherent goodness and self-sufficiency of the individual. Drawing on Romanticism and German idealism, its figures—chiefly Ralph Waldo Emerson and Henry David Thoreau—held that a deeper spiritual truth transcends the senses and is accessible directly through personal insight rather than through established institutions or received doctrine. The movement fed reform causes, from abolition to education, and reshaped American letters.
thoreau-walden: Walden records Henry David Thoreau's experiment in deliberate living, undertaken during his two years in a cabin by Walden Pond, where he sought to strip life to its essentials and confront what it had to teach. His aim was to live simply and consciously—reducing needs, observing nature closely, and resisting the distractions of a commercial society—so as to discover what is truly necessary for a meaningful existence. The book blends memoir, natural observation, and social criticism into a sustained argument for self-examined, intentional life.
civil-disobedience: Civil disobedience, as argued by Henry David Thoreau in his 1849 essay, is the deliberate, nonviolent refusal to obey unjust laws or support an unjust government, accepting the legal penalty as a form of moral protest. Prompted by his opposition to slavery and the Mexican–American War, Thoreau insisted that individual conscience outranks the dictates of the majority and that a just person may be obliged to withdraw cooperation from wrongdoing. His argument later influenced figures such as Gandhi and Martin Luther King Jr. in shaping mass movements of principled resistance.
addams-settlement: The social ethics of the settlement house is the practical moral philosophy Jane Addams developed through Hull House, the Chicago settlement she co-founded to share the lives of the urban poor and immigrant communities. Addams held that ethics must be lived and reciprocal—learned by association across class lines rather than dispensed as charity from above—and that genuine democracy requires attending to the interdependence of all members of society. Her work fused pragmatist thought with social reform, treating cooperative daily engagement as the school of a broadened, more democratic conscience.
feminism: Feminism is a broad range of intellectual and political movements united by the conviction that women have been unjustly subordinated and that the sexes deserve equal rights, opportunities, and standing. As philosophy it examines how gender shapes knowledge, power, ethics, and social institutions, and it critiques assumptions that have treated the male as the human norm. Spanning successive waves and diverse schools—liberal, socialist, radical, intersectional, and more—it shares the aim of analyzing and dismantling structures that disadvantage women.
vindication-women: A Vindication of the Rights of Woman is Mary Wollstonecraft's 1792 treatise arguing that women appear inferior to men only because they are denied education and treated as ornaments rather than rational beings. Writing amid the ideals of the Enlightenment and the French Revolution, she contended that reason is not gendered and that granting women the same intellectual and moral cultivation as men would make them better citizens, wives, and mothers. The work is a foundational text of modern feminist thought and an early systematic case for women's equality.
feminine-mystique: The Feminine Mystique names Betty Friedan's 1963 diagnosis of "the problem that has no name": the pervasive dissatisfaction of educated mid-century American housewives confined to domestic roles and told that fulfillment lay solely in marriage, motherhood, and homemaking. Friedan argued that the culture propagated an idealized image of femininity that stifled women's ambitions and identities, leaving many with an unspoken sense of emptiness. Widely credited with helping launch second-wave feminism, the book urged women to seek meaningful work and self-realization beyond the home.
